compute.reported_as: For the 36-site simulations, as well as the 108-site simulation at J2 = 0, the plain GCNN introduced in Sec. II A was able to find accurate ground and excited states. We used 4096 Monte Carlo samples and GCNNs with 4 (8) layers of 6 feature maps each for the 36- (108-) site simulations. We trained the 36-site models for 12 hours (approx. 1500 steps) and the 108-site model for 4 days (approx. 2000 steps). All simulations were carried out on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. || Sec. II A: All GCNN ansätze used in this work have a fixed number of feature maps in every layer, connected by real-valued kernels K, W. In most cases, we restrict the embedding kernels K to the local clusters shown in Fig. 1. We also impose locality on the convolutional kernels W: these are only nonzero for g = t p, where p is a point-group symmetry that leaves the origin in place, and t is a translation by a lattice vector indicated in Fig. 1. || FIG. 1. Arrangement of nonzero kernel entries for the square (left) and triangular (centre) lattices. The cross indicates the origin of the lattice and/or pure point-group symmetries. [figure, counted: triangular 3+4+5+4+3 = 19 entries, square 1+3+5+3+1 = 13 entries, cross included] || Sec. II A: The largest symmetry group for which (1b) is applicable in this basis is the direct product of the space group of the lattice and the Z2 spin parity group generated by P = prod_i sigma^x_i [42]. Irreps of this group are specified by the eigenvalue of P = ±1 and an irrep of the space group. || Sec. I: group-convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) [30,32], which allow us to impose the full space-group symmetry of the problem on the wave functions. || Sec. II A: In the output layer, we combine pairs of feature maps into complex-valued features, exponentiate them, and project the result on the desired irrep || Acknowledgments: Simulations were performed using the NetKet [24] library. || NetKet v3.8 netket/nn/symmetric_linear.py L113/L228/L348: kernel_params = self.param("kernel", self.kernel_init, (self.features, in_features, len(self.kernel_indices)), self.param_dtype); L161/L292: use_bias: bool = True; L219/L339: "bias", self.bias_init, (self.features,) || NetKet v3.8 netket/models/equivariant.py L377-L391 (GCNN_Parity_FFT): self.equivariant_layers_flip = [DenseEquivariantFFT(... use_bias=self.extra_bias and self.use_bias, ... mask=self.hidden_mask) for layer in range(self.layers - 1)]; L322: extra_bias: bool = False || NetKet v3.8 test/models/test_gcnn.py L101-L140 test_gcnn_mask: assert vstate1.n_parameters - vstate2.n_parameters == 4; assert vstate1.n_parameters - vstate3.n_parameters == 16 || v1 (arXiv:2211.07749v1 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.07749v1 (route2a-fetched/2211.07749v1.pdf)) Sec. IV: The simulations is this section were performed using GCNNs with 6 features per layer, 4 (8) layers and 8192 (4096) samples per SR iteration for the 36- (108-)site simulations.

compute.note: Plain GCNN with 8 layers of 6 feature maps for the 108-site J2 = 0 cluster; parameter count not stated. Steps are "approx. 2000". GPU-hours not stated for this run (only the wall-clock on one A100). || parameters = 115074 evaluated (8-layer plain GCNN, 108-site triangular, point group C6v order 12): NetKet GCNN with spin parity and input/hidden masks = embedding F*n_in + F bias + (L-1) equivariant layers (F^2*n_h + F bias) + (L-1) parity-flip layers (F^2*n_h, no bias, extra_bias=False default) with F = 6 feature maps, L = 8 layers, n_in = 19 kernel sites (Fig. 1, origin included), n_h = 19 x |point group| 12 = 228: 120 + 57498 + 57456 = 115074. Real parameters ("real-valued kernels"), counted the way NetKet's n_parameters counts them (unmasked entries only, NetKet >= 3.7). Independent of N and of |G|: the masked kernels depend only on the cluster size and the point-group order, so the count changes across rows only through the depth L. Assumptions and their size: (i) spin parity doubles the hidden kernels (the paper's symmetry group is space group x Z2 parity and it labels irreps with ±; without the parity-flip layers the count would be 57618); (ii) biases are the NetKet default use_bias=True (48 parameters; not stated in the paper); (iii) "in most cases" the embedding is local; a full-range embedding (n_in = 108) would give 115608; (iv) with NetKet < 3.7 (e.g. at v1, Nov 2022) masked kernels were stored full-size (F x F x |G|) and multiplied by the mask, so n_parameters would print a larger number of which only the above are free. Consistency check: LayerSR (App. C) requires fewer samples than parameters per layer; with parity one triangular layer pair has 2 x 6 x 6 x 228 + 6 = 16422 parameters, just above the 16384 samples used there, without parity 8214 would not be. Existing samples = 4096 and iterations = 2000 checked against v2 Sec. IV: both are the 108-site J2 = 0 ground-state run (energy -0.55315(3) x 432 = row energy); v1 also states 4096 samples for 108 sites (v1 energy -0.5531(4), an earlier run). Kept.

compute.reported_as: Appendix A9 Optimization parameters: We optimized all models using IT-SWO[25]. We used 30 iterations in the inner loop and chose imaginary time constant β based on the relative scale of the energy spectrum for different problems (Table V: Triangular N=108, β = 0.01). Each iteration was performed using adam optimizer[24] with b1 = 0.9; b2 = 0.99 and learning rate that was decayed exponentially with the rate of 0.1 over 8∗10^5 updates starting with 7∗10^−4 ... We optimized all GNN models for 8∗10^5 iterations (≈ 26000 IT-SWO steps). For larger system sizes we initialized the weights with values from smaller system sizes. ... All models were optimized using Google's Cloud TPU v4. All models trained within a day. ... Appendix A8b: All results were computed using MCMC using 2∗10^5 samples from equilibrated Markov chains. ... Appendix A8c: To measure computational efficiency we have timed the process of evaluating 7200 batches of 32 basis configuration within a MCMC process. The GNN-2 model took 17.4 seconds to accomplish this task, while our unstructured ResNet baseline finishes in 2.14 seconds. ... Appendix A6a: Node and edge functions of the Encoder, Processor and Decoder are implemented as MLPs with 3 hidden layers with ReLU activations. The node and edge embeddings have size 64, while hidden layers width 128. We use 6 message passing steps with residual connections in the Processor. || Sec. III Architecture: "The encoder maps nodes and edges of input graph X to latent features of width 64. Next, the processor performs M rounds of message passing, updating the graph as Gt = Gt−1 +GNt(Gt−1). The residual GraphNet blocks GNt [41] use MLP node and edge functions. The decoder computes the final latent edge and node features Y from GM, by processing them using a MLP." | "Nodes vi are initialized by concatenating c and s, and edges ejk between interacting spins are initialized to zero. The sublattice encoding s is a one-hot vector" | "we obtain scalar outputs by sum-pooling the latent features over nodes and edges; concatenating the results into a single vector Z of size 128; and processing it with a linear layer. ... (2) GNN-2, an ansatz which computes each output using a separate network with output size of one." || App. A6a: "The final linear layer maps 128-dimensional latent vector to 2(1) outputs for GNN(GNN-2) models." || App. A6b: "our selective experiments show that using shared weights in the processor module generally achieves similar performance to the unshared variation." || App. A7a Table III: Triangular "≤ 0.14" -> "Coplanar" (Fig. 8 'Coplanar' panel shows three colours) || App. A9: "During training we use the same MCMC parameters as for evaluation discussed in Appendix A2." || App. A2: "For efficiency we maintain a batch of MCMC chains, which evolves throughout optimization. We follow the rule of thumb of performing N MCMC steps between sampling from the chain to reduce autocorrelation effects, where N is equal to the number of degrees of freedom." (no chain count or batch size given)

Blanket statements for all models: 8×10^5 Adam updates (≈26000 IT-SWO outer steps) on Google Cloud TPU v4, 'all models trained within a day' (an upper bound, recorded as wall_clock); number of TPU chips/cores not stated; larger systems were warm-started from smaller-system weights. samples = 2×10^5 MCMC samples used for the reported energy evaluation; the training batch/chain count is not stated numerically. No parameter count stated (architecture: embeddings 64, MLP hidden width 128, 3 hidden layers, 6 message-passing steps). Timing 17.4 s per 7200×32 evaluations is a relative-efficiency benchmark with unnamed hardware. || route2a kochkov-gnn (2026-09-24): parameters NOT counted. Stated: 64-wide node/edge latents, MLPs with 3 hidden layers of 128 + ReLU, 6 residual message-passing steps, decoder MLP, sum-pool of nodes and edges to Z of size 128 (so decoder outputs 64), final linear 128->1 per network, GNN-2 = two separate networks. Unstated, so no count: (1) whether processor weights are shared across the 6 steps (GN_t notation and A6b suggest unshared by default, but not said); (2) width of the zero-initialised input edge features; (3) LayerNorm or not (DeepMind encode-process-decode codes usually have it; the paper does not mention it); (4) whether the GraphNet blocks have a global block/features; (5) whether the one-hot sublattice vector has length 3 (Coplanar, Fig. 8) or a fixed padded length; (6) whether GNN-2's two networks are both full encode-process-decode stacks. Conditional evaluation for scale only (NOT a value): MLP(in) = 128·in+128 + 2·(128·128+128) + (128·64+64) = 128·in + 41408; per network = MLP(4) + MLP(1) + 6·[MLP(192) + MLP(128)] + 2·MLP(64) + 129 = 41920 + 41536 + 6·(65984 + 57792) + 99200 + 129 = 925,441; GNN-2 = 1,850,882 (unshared processor, 1-wide edge input, no LayerNorm, no globals); shared processor gives 306,561 per network, 613,122 for GNN-2; LayerNorm adds 2048 per network. Parameter count does not depend on N (all MLPs shared over nodes and edges; the sublattice one-hot is an input, not a learned per-site embedding), so the 36- and 108-site models have the same count for the same sublattice encoding. FLAG samples: 200000 is the Appendix A8b final-evaluation count ('All results were computed using MCMC using 2∗10^5 samples'); the per-step training sample count (number of chains/batch) is not stated; A9 only says training uses 'the same MCMC parameters as for evaluation discussed in Appendix A2', and A2 gives no number. The previous harvest reading (compute-harvest/fetched/parts/2110.06390.json) set samples null for this reason. Kept 200000 per rule 8 (no contradicting number), but it does not meet DATA.md's per-step definition; recommend null. FLAG iterations: 8×10^5 counts Adam updates (30 inner updates per IT-SWO outer step, ≈26000 outer steps); whether each update draws fresh MCMC samples or the 30 inner updates reuse one sample set is not stated, so iterations × samples may overcount sampling by up to 30×. The run was warm-started from a smaller-size model (A9: 'For larger system sizes we initialized the weights with values from smaller system sizes'); that pre-training is not counted. Table IV lists no smaller triangular J2 = 0 run, so the warm-start source of this 108-site model is not stated. || Ruling 2026-09-24: samples = 200000 is the final evaluation's count, not per optimisation step (DATA.md), so null.
